content: Pre-labor, also referred to as Prodromal Labor, represents the initial signs that occur before the onset of active labor. It is essentially the body's preparatory phase for true labor. Despite being commonly misnamed as false labor, prodromal labor is a distinct physiological process. It often begins in a manner similar to traditional labor but does not progress to the delivery of the baby. Not all pregnant individuals experience this stage of labor in a noticeable way, even though it occurs universally. However, this does not imply that every woman will exhibit all the associated symptoms. The term prodromal labor is used to describe a collection of physical changes that may occur in a pregnant woman prior to the initiation of active labor. These changes can include an increase in blood volume, which may sometimes lead to swelling (edema), the occurrence of Braxton Hicks contractions, the presence of colostrum in the breasts, and the expulsion of the mucus plug that has sealed the cervix throughout the pregnancy. The term false labor is occasionally used to describe a series of Braxton Hicks contractions that are mistakenly interpreted as true labor.
